mainEntity.name: Is Kuma a native meditation app for iPhone Duo?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Kuma is built with SwiftUI and includes fold-aware meditation and reflection layouts for iPhone Duo on iOS 27.1 or later. The timer and practice controls adapt to the inner display while compact iPhones keep a single-column layout. Duo layouts have been checked in the simulator; physical-device validation is pending. The public beta is in preparation.

mainEntity.name: Does Kuma work on other iPhones?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Kuma supports iPhone with iOS 18 or later. The fold-aware Duo layout requires iOS 27.1 or later, but the meditation timer, personal practice log, offline written guide, and widgets are also available on supported compact iPhones.

mainEntity.name: How is Kuma different from apps like Insight Timer?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you want a wide library of guided sessions, an app like Insight Timer may suit you. Kuma focuses on self-directed practice: a flexible timer, an illustrated companion, a weekly rhythm, and your personal log. Its offline guide offers written teachings and reflections rather than an audio catalog.

mainEntity.name: Do I need an account or an Apple Watch?

acceptedAnswer.text: Neither. Solo practice works without signing in. Cloud backup and Apple Health are optional, and you can use Kuma entirely on your iPhone. The optional Watch companion requires watchOS 11 or later.

mainEntity.name: When can I try the beta?

acceptedAnswer.text: The public TestFlight beta is being prepared. Join the email list above and we’ll send the installation details when external testing is available. Signing up does not install the app or guarantee a release date.

mainEntity.name: What if I miss a day?

acceptedAnswer.text: Kuma starts with a flexible weekly aspiration, so you can build a rhythm that makes room for life. Any completed session counts as practice that day, including a short one. You can choose a strict daily streak in Settings if that’s helpful to you.

Kuma is a quiet companion for your practice. His round, legless body recalls a Daruma doll, the Japanese figure inspired by Bodhidharma and associated with perseverance. His circular form also echoes the ensō of Zen brush painting—a simple expression of practice, presence, and space. (Daruma, Ensō)

His white color is a nod to the upāsaka, a lay Buddhist practitioner. The Pāli Canon describes white-clad lay followers practicing amid everyday life. Kuma carries that spirit: a little company as you sit, return, and begin again. (DN 29)
